newsitem.title: UK: British election leaves financial markets cold.
newsitem.headline: British election leaves financial markets cold.

text.p: Britain's financial markets are hard put to summon any enthusiasm for the election campaign and only a drop in the opposition Labour Party's big lead will shake them from torpor, economists and traders say.

U.S. interest rates and jobs data have overshadowed the tidal wave of election media coverage in the past three weeks and a rogue UK inflation figure next week would be much more market-moving than anything the politicians can throw up.

"The campaign is having minimal impact in the City," said Michael O'Hanlon, chief international economist at PaineWebber. "If you wanted to quantify it, it's less than 10 percent as important as say a non-farm payroll figure."

Equity and bond markets worldwide were hamstrung last week, awaiting the release of key U.S. jobs figures on Friday. Few investors were willing to take sizeable positions beforehand, particularly since the Federal Reserve forced through a rate rise, the first in more than two years, the week before.

The FTSE-100 index of leading UK shares, for instance, began last week at 4,205 and closed just 11 points higher on Thursday night, on the eve of the employment report -- despite the release of election manifestos by the ruling Conservatives and Labour on Wednesday and Thursday.
It is the fear of further U.S. rate rises that is keeping bonds and shares on the back foot. The election, on May 1, can take a back seat, traders say.

"Politics is no longer a concern for domestic investors and as far as the foreigners are concerned, they don't give a damn who wins. They see little difference between the two main parties," said one senior government bonds salesman.

O'Hanlon said there could be a few policy implications on offer for those prepared to sift through the blanket media coverage and political point-scoring. "But nothing will change the grand scheme of things."
For the markets, Europe is the key factor. "And none of them have a definitive view on that," O'Hanlon said.

Both the Conservatives and Labour Party are keeping their options open on whether to join European economic and monetary union in the first wave, scheduled for January 1999. But both say it is extremely unlikely Britain would sign up then.

The pound has benefitted from Britain's aloofness over EMU, soaring to 4-1/2 year highs against the mark and back into its old exchange rate mechanism band. But the political rhetoric has had little do with that.
"I've certainly reached the point where I switch off," the gilts salesman said.

For the stock market, details of a utilities windfall tax planned by Labour could move certain shares. But since shadow finance minister Gordon Brown will not announce which companies will have to pay up until an emergency budget some weeks after the election, all they can do is wait.
One of the problems is that Labour, 20 points and more ahead in the polls and hot favourite to take power for the first time in 18 years, is playing it safe on policy.

Mistakes in front of the media's unblinking eye are not acceptable, so those looking for clues to economic policy hear only a string of mantras -- national economic interest, spend only to invest, no income tax rises, a referendum on EMU. "We've heard it all before, and before that, and before that again," one currency trader said.
But the last thing the markets want to see now is a narrowing of Labour's lead, despite the fact many in London's square mile would love to see a Tory government returned.

"A hung parliament would be a nightmare scenario," said Mees Pierson futures broker Jonathon York. "If the Tories started to come back in the polls and squeezed Labour's lead to five-10 percent, then gilts would get hurt quite a bit."
A hung parliament, where no party holds an overall majority, would mean political logjam and uncertainty. But there are no signs so far of Labour's yawning lead being chipped away.
"If the Tories closed the gap it would become more serious," O'Hanlon said. "I still think the result may be much closer than the polls suggest. But not close enough to wake us all up."
